name: Hair restorer tonic (Brylcreem era)

lead: Hair restorer tonics were over-the-counter lotions, oils and creams marketed from the 1800s onward to bring back lost hair or thicken thinning hair. They shared shelves with grooming products such as Rowland's Macassar oil and later Brylcreem.

The payoff buyers wanted was a fuller-looking head of hair. Grooming oils and creams do add shine and let hair be styled to look neater; regrowth claims were another matter, and one randomised trial of a Chinese herbal restorer found a small difference from placebo.

paras: Users rubbed a liquid or cream into the scalp or hair, usually daily, sometimes with a massage. Styling creams like Brylcreem were used on combed hair for hold and shine rather than growth.

Reported harms include irritant and allergic contact dermatitis from plant saps and ingredients such as glycyrrhizic acid, and a 19th-century committee report on a death from a hair restorer. Modern regrowth treatments are separate, regulated products.

lead: Hair restorer tonics were patent preparations sold from the 19th century to restore or grow hair. Alexander Rowland of London began selling Rowland's Macassar Oil around 1793, advertised with extravagant claims; a c. 1814 Rowlandson illustration mocked the claim that it would grow hair on balding men [1].

Brylcreem followed in 1928, made by County Chemicals in Birmingham as an emulsion of water and mineral oil stabilised with beeswax, noted for its shine [2]. It was a styling cream; its place in this entry is as the best-known product of the era's grooming market.

People used tonics to look fuller-haired and well groomed. Research is sparse: a randomised double-blind trial of the herbal restorer Dabao in 396 men found a small difference over placebo in hair count [3], and case reports document reactions [4][5].

paras: Macassar oil was used by Western European men from the 1800s into the early 1900s; Rowland's was among the first nationally advertised products [1]. It transferred to furniture, which prompted antimacassar cloths [1]. A report titled Death from the Use of Hair Restorer appeared in the Chicago Medical Journal in 1870 [6].
Brylcreem's 1939 print ads used an RAF airman, and RAF personnel in WWII were nicknamed Brylcreem boys [2]. Ownership passed through Beecham, Sara Lee (1993) and Unilever (2012) [2].

In a 1991 randomised double-blind trial, 396 men with androgenetic alopecia used the Chinese herb extract Dabao or placebo for six months. Hair counts rose in both groups, by 133 versus 109 hairs per 5 square centimetres, a difference of 24 (p=0.03 one-sided); the authors described the cosmetic effect as modest but real [3].
Case reports describe irritant contact dermatitis after agave sap was used as a hair restorer [4] and allergic contact dermatitis from glycyrrhizic acid in a restorer [5].
